Need to search first.I've written notes for 28–35, 38, 42 and 46–48. Partway through, the research tools hit their usage limit and stopped working. Because of that, I have **nothing for vv. 36–37, 39–41, 43–45 and 49–53**. Nothing I found came from netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, oca.org, Lutheran sites or prosperity/word-of-faith teaching either. I also couldn't open whole pages. Everything below comes from the search-result text of each page. Where a Biblehub or StudyLight page didn't show which commentator wrote something, I've said "unnamed" rather than guess.

---

**v. 28 – "Greetings, highly favored… The Lord is with you"**

*Traditional reading*
- Barnes: "Hail" is a greeting like "peace" or "joy be with you." She is "highly favored" because she will be the mother of the long-awaited Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- Matthew Poole: the word for "hail" means "rejoice," or something like "God save thee." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-28.htm
- Benson: the same favour was said of Noah, Moses and David. "The Lord is with thee" was said to Gideon (Judges 6:12), and "blessed above women" to Jael (Judges 5:24). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-28.htm
- Gill: "the Lord is with thee" was a normal Jewish greeting (Ruth 2:4). The favour is not the saving grace all believers share, but her being singled out to be the Messiah's mother. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/luke/1-28.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- Matthew Henry: she was chosen not for any merit of her own but out of free grace. We are not to pray to her, but we should praise God for her. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- Calvin: Gabriel opens a hard-to-believe message by praising God's grace, which lifts her mind to God's boundless kindness. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- Enduring Word (Guzik): Gabriel says three things: she is highly favored, the Lord is with her, and she is blessed. All three are also true of believers (Eph 1:6; Matt 28:20; Eph 1:3). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- Text note (unnamed commentary): the words "blessed art thou among women" are missing from many of the best manuscripts. The Pulpit sermon page thinks they were borrowed from Elizabeth's words in v. 42. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-28.htm ; https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/1-28.htm

*Protestant–Catholic difference*
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the same word appears only once elsewhere, in Ephesians 1:6 ("made accepted"). They call the Latin Vulgate's "full of grace" a mistranslation that the Roman Church has exploited. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-28.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-30.htm
- Adam Clarke (StudyLight tags him Wesleyan/Methodist): she was chosen above all women to bear the Messiah. He rejects "mother of God" outright. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/luke/1-28.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-29.html
- Coffman, citing Plummer: "full of grace" is wrong if it means grace she gives out, and right only if it means grace she received. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- GotQuestions: the word means "much grace," God's undeserved favour. The verse doesn't claim she was sinless. https://www.gotquestions.org/virgin-Mary.html ; https://www.gotquestions.org/was-Mary-sinless.html
- Catholic view (Catholic Answers): *kecharitomene* is a perfect passive participle. It means grace already given and still lasting, used like a new name. They read it as pointing to the Immaculate Conception (Mary conceived without sin). https://www.catholic.com/bible-navigator/mary%E2%80%99s-immaculate-conception/luke128 ; https://www.catholic.com/qa/full-of-grace-versus-highly-favored
- Catholic Answers on the Ephesians 1:6 objection: the two verb forms use different stems. Luke's perfect form suggests "enduringly endowed with grace." https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/cris-attack-on-mary-part-ii

**v. 29 – Mary troubled**
- Clarke: she was amazed at the angel's glory and puzzled about what his words meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-29.html
- Howard Marshall (quoted in the Light of Israel commentary): she wondered at being greeted in such exalted terms, as one chosen and empowered to serve God like the great Old Testament figures. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-30.html
- Matthew Henry: when she didn't answer, the angel paused and then went on to reassure her. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-29.html

**v. 30 – "Do not be afraid… you have found favor"**
- Ellicott's *Commentary for English Readers*: the noun is the usual word for "grace." "Favour" is the better translation here because "grace" carries technical theological baggage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-30.htm
- Barnes: the angel brings good news. Her favour is being chosen as the Messiah's mother. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-30.htm
- Utley (quoted in Light of Israel): the Greek means "stop being afraid," halting a fear already under way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-30.html
- Biblehub Study Bible: the favour comes from God's choice, not her merit. It's like Noah (Gen 6:8) and Moses (Ex 33:12). https://biblehub.com/study/luke/1-30.htm
- A difference in emphasis:
  - GotQuestions stresses her privilege, not her piety: the favour says more about God's goodness than about Mary. https://www.gotquestions.org/why-did-God-choose-Mary.html
  - Coffman suggests her knowledge of Scripture, trust and virtuous life were the usual conditions for receiving such favour. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-30.html

**v. 31 – The name Jesus**
- Bible.org: Jesus is the same name as the Hebrew Joshua. He fulfils the Old Testament picture of Joshua. https://bible.org/seriespage/5-greatest-birth-announcement-ever-unto-us-son-given-luke-126-38
- Unnamed devotional commentary: "Jesus" means Saviour. The name means little to people until they see their guilt. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-30.htm

**vv. 32–33 – Son of the Most High; David's throne**
- Desiring God (Piper): the titles show that the person God became was both divine and human. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-child-to-be-born-will-be-called-holy-the-son-of-god
- Matthew Henry: though born in lowly circumstances, he would be given David's throne. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html

**v. 34 – "How can this be?"**
- Enduring Word: it's the same question Zechariah asked (1:18). His came from doubt; hers from faith full of wonder. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 35 – The Spirit will overshadow you**
- Calvin:
  - The angel doesn't explain how, so as not to feed curiosity.
  - "Come upon" marks an extraordinary work with no natural means.
  - "Overshadow" suggests a hidden work, as if behind a cloud, to be met with reverence.
  https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31.ix.vii.html
- Bengel (via Vincent and Biblehub): the gentlest working of God's power, so the divine fire made Mary fruitful without consuming her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-35.htm
- Constable and Coffman: the word recalls the cloud over the tabernacle (Ex 40:35), the Transfiguration cloud, and the Spirit hovering in Genesis 1:2. This is a new creation. Constable says it is nothing like pagan stories of gods and women. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-35.html
- Utley (quoted in Light of Israel): it was not a sexual act; the image is the Shekinah cloud, God's visible presence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-35.html
- Gill: some see the Spirit "brooding" as in Genesis 1:2; others see a bridal canopy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-35.html
- Matthew Henry: it is often assumed she conceived at this moment, but Scripture is silent, so we shouldn't be dogmatic. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-35.html
- Piper: this "holy" child is pure and without defect. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-child-to-be-born-will-be-called-holy-the-son-of-god
- Bible.org: the Spirit who gave life at creation creates life in a virgin. https://bible.org/seriespage/5-greatest-birth-announcement-ever-unto-us-son-given-luke-126-38

*Protestant–Catholic difference*
- Protestant view:
  - An unnamed older commentary says the Spirit sanctified the part of the virgin's flesh that formed Christ's body. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-35.htm
  - A sermon on Biblehub argues that if anyone besides Christ had been made pure first, that person, not Christ, would be the source of renewed humanity. https://biblehub.com/sermons/luke/1-35.htm
- Catholic view: the Spirit purified and filled Mary herself at her own conception. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/what-it-means-to-be-virgin-of-virgins

**v. 38 – "I am the Lord's servant"**
- Calvin: she stops arguing and makes herself obey. Holding one's mind captive to God's word is true faith; arguing back is "the mother of unbelief." https://biblehub.com/library/calvin/commentary_on_matthew_mark_luke_volume_1/luke_1_34-38.htm
- Unnamed commentary: hers was the language of faith, and she asked for no sign. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-30.htm
- Enduring Word: we don't know exactly when Jesus was conceived. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/
- GotQuestions: an example of total devotion. https://www.gotquestions.org/why-did-God-choose-Mary.html
- Precept Austin (Luke 2 page): from then on her life was part of the fulfilment of prophecy. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-2-commentary
- Catholic view: links "handmaid of the Lord" to God's promise to pour out his Spirit on his handmaids. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/bible-mary-conceived-without-sin

**v. 42 – "Blessed are you among women"**
- Gill: other women would call her blessed, as Elizabeth does here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/1-28.htm
- GotQuestions:
  - Catholics use this verse (with v. 28) for Mary's sinlessness, but being blessed doesn't require being sinless. https://www.gotquestions.org/was-Mary-sinless.html
  - The verse is part of the Hail Mary prayer. https://www.gotquestions.org/Hail-Mary.html

**v. 46 – "My soul magnifies the Lord"**
- Enduring Word: Mary was highly privileged and did what blessed people should do: she magnified the Lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-1/

**v. 47 – "God my Savior"**
- GotQuestions: a sinless person wouldn't need a Savior. https://www.gotquestions.org/was-Mary-sinless.html
- Precept Austin, Luke 2 page: her later sin offering fits with her being a sinner who needed a Savior (citing 1:47). https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-2-commentary

**v. 48 – Humble state; "all generations will call me blessed"**
- Matthew Henry: Mary herself explains the angel's "blessed" here. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- Light of Israel: the truth is real but, it says, has been "greatly perverted" in Roman Catholicism. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/1-28.html
- Biblehub: choosing a lowly servant fits God's pattern of using the weak (1 Cor 1:27). https://biblehub.com/luke/1-30.htm

---

The notes lean on older and evangelical commentators. I found no clear Protestant-versus-Protestant split, and I couldn't check the Lutheran or Orthodox angles, or what Catholics say about v. 43. To finish the job, the next things to read would be Enduring Word for Luke 1:39–56, the Biblehub and StudyLight commentary pages for each missing verse, and the netbible.org notes on Luke 1.
